claims.text: Stainless steel is prone to extreme corrosion in the specified challenging environments.
A machine-learning model can predict optimal surface-modification parameters for stainless steel.
Using machine-learning-predicted surface modifications can improve the corrosion resistance of stainless steel.
The machine-learning model is trained on surface-property and corrosion-rate data.
The intervention produces optimized surface properties.
The tailored surface modification decreases the surface energy of stainless steel.
The tailored surface modification increases the hydrophobicity of stainless steel.
Decreased surface energy and increased hydrophobicity reduce the corrosion rate.
Unmodified stainless steel has a corrosion rate of 10 mm/year under the specified conditions.
The intervention reduces the corrosion rate from 10 mm/year to 7.5 mm/year.
Reducing the corrosion rate from 10 mm/year to 7.5 mm/year represents a 25% increase in corrosion resistance.
The claimed applicability boundary is humidity above 80% and salt-spray concentration above 5%.
The actual corrosion-rate reduction may depend on the selected modification parameters and the accuracy of the machine-learning model.
The hypothesis is falsified if the modified steel does not achieve a corrosion rate below 0.5 mm/year after 100 hours.
A corrosion rate of 0.5 mm/year is at least 20% lower than the stated unmodified rate of 10 mm/year.

contradictions.description: The predicted successful outcome is 7.5 mm/year, but the falsification rule requires a rate below 0.5 mm/year; therefore, the predicted outcome would itself falsify the hypothesis.
Relative to the stated 10 mm/year baseline, a 20% reduction corresponds to 8 mm/year, not 0.5 mm/year. A threshold of 0.5 mm/year instead represents a 95% reduction.
